reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant late-onset distal myopathy caused by a founder variant in TIA1, most prevalent in Swedish and Finnish populations
Onset is typically in the fifth decade or later, distinguishing it from the early-onset distal myopathies
Weakness and clumsiness begin in the finger and hand extensors, initially impairing fine finger movements, before spreading to the small hand muscles and the lower legs
Slow progression usually allows preserved ambulation, and the phenotype is generally milder in heterozygotes than in the rare homozygous cases
TIA1 encodes an RNA-binding stress-granule protein, linking Welander myopathy mechanistically to the rimmed-vacuole myopathy spectrum
Creatine kinase is normal or mildly raised and electromyography shows myopathic changes, sometimes with irritable features
Muscle biopsy characteristically shows rimmed vacuoles with protein aggregation on a chronic myopathic background
Diagnosis combines the distinctive adult-onset hand-extensor weakness pattern with TIA1 genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Welander distal myopathy is caused by a dominant founder variant in TIA1, which encodes an RNA-binding protein that nucleates stress granules involved in the cellular response to stress. The mutation is thought to alter stress-granule dynamics and RNA handling, promoting accumulation of misfolded and aggregated proteins within muscle fibres. This produces the rimmed vacuoles and protein deposits seen on biopsy and places the disorder within the broader family of rimmed-vacuolar myopathies, with the earliest and most severe involvement in the distal upper-limb muscles.
additionalDifferentials: Other rimmed-vacuole distal myopathies (GNE myopathy, Udd myopathy)
Distal spinal muscular atrophy or motor neuropathy affecting the hands
Ulnar or other focal peripheral neuropathy affecting hand function
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy seeking rimmed vacuoles and protein aggregates
Muscle MRI to characterise the distal-predominant involvement
Targeted TIA1 testing or a distal myopathy gene panel
Family history assessment and evaluation of relatives given dominant inheritance
redFlags: Rapid progression or prominent proximal weakness suggesting inclusion body myositis or another diagnosis
Dysphagia or respiratory involvement not typical of classic Welander myopathy
Asymmetric quadriceps weakness raising suspicion of inclusion body myositis
Early severe disability suggesting a homozygous or alternative genotype
reference.prognosis: The disorder progresses slowly over years to decades and heterozygous patients usually retain functional independence with a normal or near-normal lifespan; the rare homozygous form is considerably more severe with earlier and more widespread weakness.
pitfalls: Confusing it with inclusion body myositis, which shares rimmed vacuoles but has a different weakness pattern and no family history
Attributing hand weakness to a focal neuropathy and missing the myopathy
Assuming normal creatine kinase excludes muscle disease
Overlooking the characteristic founder-population family history
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: With no disease-modifying therapy available, focus management on supportive measures that preserve function
Provide physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain hand dexterity and mobility, with aids and adaptations for impaired fine finger movements
Prescribe ankle-foot orthoses for lower-leg weakness and address falls risk as distal involvement progresses
Monitor the slowly progressive weakness periodically, reassuring that ambulation is usually preserved in heterozygotes
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant condition and assess at-risk relatives
Coordinate care through a neuromuscular multidisciplinary team, escalating support if the rare, more severe homozygous phenotype is suspected
